title: What a Buyer's Roof Inspection Shows
description: A home inspector has an hour. A roof inspection is the deck, the flashing, and the attic, photographed, before you waive the option.
html:
The home inspection report will say “roof appears serviceable” or “recommend a roofer.” That sentence is not a roof report. The inspector is covering the whole house. The roof gets a look from the eaves, maybe a few steps up, and a glance in the attic if the hatch is not buried.

What we photograph

  • Every slope, plus hips, valleys, and the chimney or wall flashing.
  • Pipe boots and the seal around them.
  • Soft spots underfoot, and how widespread they are.
  • The attic: stained decking, rusty nails, wet insulation, fans that never leave the attic.
  • How many layers are on the house.

You get pictures, not a shrug. A buyer can price a cracked boot. A buyer cannot price “monitor.” Sellers can fix the small things before they become a credit request.

Before you waive anything

If the report flags the roof, use the option period for a real roof inspection. We work that clock. If the roof is fine, you stop wondering. If it needs a roof replacement, you still have time to ask the seller to do it, credit it, or let you walk.

What a credit request should be based on

Ask for a number tied to a photo. A cracked pipe boot is a repair with a price. A slope of soft deck is a replacement with a price. “Roof may need attention” is not a number, and it is how option periods turn into arguments. If we write the report, the buyer’s agent and the listing agent are looking at the same pictures.

We are not the home inspector and we are not the appraiser. We are the crew that would have to fix what the photo shows. That is the opinion worth having before you waive the roof.
